segments.say: Lesson 15. Design a U R L Shortener (bit.ly). Key generation, base62, a 100:1 read-heavy path, 301 versus 302 redirects, caching and analytics.

Design a service like bit.ly: turn long U R Ls into short codes and redirect anyone who opens the short link, at huge read volume. Here is an analogy. A cloakroom ticket for links: hand in a long U R L, get a short ticket; anyone with the ticket is sent straight to the original.

Why does this matter? The classic first design question: small, but covers I Ds, caching, databases and scale. A few key words. Short code: for example aZ3x9Q, the unique key. Base62: Encoding with 0–9, a–z, A–Z. 301 / 302: Permanent / temporary redirect. Read-heavy: Far more reads than writes.
Create & redirect paths. Shorten a long U R L leads to sho.rt/aZ3x9Q, redirect fast, optional custom alias and expiry, click analytics. Assume 100M new U R Ls/month and 100:1 reads to writes.
Writes about 100M / 2.5M s about 40/s. Reads about 4k/s (peaks ~20k). 5 years about 6B U R Ls times ~500 B about 3 T B. 7 base62 chars equals 62 to the 7 about 3.5 trillion codes, plenty.
Key generation: a key-generation service hands out pre-generated unique I Ds (or a counter / Snowflake I D leads to base62 encode). No collisions and no "check if exists" loop.
Store code leads to long url, owner, created, expiry in a K V / no sequel store. Simple lookups by primary key, easy to shard by code.
Redirect path: check the cache first. 20% of links get ~80% of the traffic, so the hit ratio is high.
Miss leads to D B leads to populate cache leads to respond 301 (permanent, browsers cache it, less load) or 302 (temporary, every click hits us, better analytics).
Emit click events asynchronously to Kafka leads to stream processing leads to analytics store. Never slow the redirect for analytics.

A P I & data model. P O S T /api/v1/urls long url, custom alias?, expires at? leads to short url. G E T / code, giving 301/302 with Location header. Table: code (P K), long url, user id, created at, expires at. Optional index on long url to dedupe.

Key generation options. Hash (MD5/S H A) of U R L, take 7 chars: collisions are possible, so check and retry. The same U R L gives the same code (dedupe). Counter plus base62: unique and short. A global counter is a bottleneck, so use ranges per server (ZooKeeper hands out blocks) or Snowflake-style I Ds. Sequential codes are guessable; shuffle if that matters. Pre-generated key service: offline-generate random codes into a "unused" table, and servers grab batches. Fast, no collisions.

Deep-dive talking points. Hot links: cache plus C D N edge redirects. Abuse: rate-limit creation, scan for malware or phishing U R Ls. Expiry: lazy delete on read plus a background cleanup job. Custom aliases: uniqueness check with a conditional insert.

Say it in the interview. "It's a read-heavy K V problem: ~40 writes/s versus ~4k reads/s. I'd generate unique 7-char base62 codes from a key service or a range-allocated counter, store code leads to U R L in a sharded K V store, serve redirects through a cache with a high hit rate, return 302 if analytics matter or 301 to save load, and push click events to Kafka asynchronously.".
Let's compare. Browser caches?: yes, no. Server load: lower, higher. Analytics accuracy: misses repeat clicks, every click counted. Change destination later: hard, easy.

Key generation. Hash plus truncate: possible leads to retry, none, dedupes same U R L. Counter plus base62: none, counter ranges / Snowflake, guessable sequence. Pre-generated keys: none, key D B, fastest, simple at runtime.

A likely interview question: Design a U R L shortener in 60 seconds. A strong answer: Read-heavy (100:1). Unique 7-char base62 codes from a key service or counter ranges. K V store sharded by code. Cache in front for hot links. 302 for analytics or 301 for less load. Async click events to Kafka. Rate-limit creation and scan for abuse.
That's it for Design a U R L Shortener (bit.ly). Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
